description: Magnetic poles, Earth's magnetism, Faraday's law, Lenz's law, electromagnets

questions.stem: The SI unit of magnetic field strength (B, magnetic flux density) is:
questions.explanation: Tesla (T) — magnetic flux DENSITY, named after Nikola Tesla. 1 T = 1 Wb/m² = 1 N/(A·m). Earth's magnetic field at the surface ≈ 25-65 µT. Refrigerator magnet ~5 mT. Hospital MRI ~1.5-3 T. Strongest steady lab field ~45 T. Other related units — Weber (Wb) = magnetic FLUX (= T·m²); Henry (H) = inductance (= Wb/A); Gauss (CGS, 1 T = 10⁴ Gauss).

questions.stem: Magnetic field lines around a bar magnet:

options.option_text: Start from south pole and end at north
Form closed loops; emerge from N pole, enter S pole outside the magnet, run S→N inside

questions.explanation: Magnetic field lines form closed loops — no monopoles in classical magnetism (Maxwell's 2nd equation: ∇·B = 0). Outside magnet: from N to S; inside: from S to N. Lines never cross. Density of lines indicates field strength. The 'isolated magnetic monopole' has been hypothesised (Dirac, 1931) but never observed experimentally despite decades of searches.

questions.stem: The geographic North Pole of Earth is actually the:

options.option_text: Magnetic South Pole of Earth (since opposite poles attract — a compass north points there)
Both Magnetic North and Magnetic South simultaneously

questions.explanation: A compass needle's NORTH end points to geographic North → that point must be a MAGNETIC SOUTH (opposites attract). So the geographic North Pole is technically a magnetic 'south' pole, and vice versa. The terminology 'Magnetic North Pole' commonly used in geomagnetic context is a convention. Earth's magnetic field also drifts ('polar wandering') and reverses on geological timescales (last full reversal ~780,000 years ago). Magnetic field generated by molten outer-core convection — 'geodynamo'.

questions.stem: Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction states that an EMF is induced in a circuit:

options.option_text: When the magnetic flux through it changes with time

questions.explanation: Faraday's Law: EMF = −dΦ_B/dt where Φ_B is magnetic flux. The minus sign represents Lenz's law (induced EMF opposes the change). Discovered 1831 by Michael Faraday and independently by Joseph Henry. Forms the basis of generators, transformers, induction cooktops, electric motors. AC generators rotate a coil in a magnetic field — flux varies sinusoidally → AC EMF. DC generators add a commutator to flip current direction every half-cycle.

questions.topic: Magnetism and magnetic field — mixed tiers

options.option_text: Direction of induced current — opposes the cause that produced it

questions.explanation: Lenz's law (1834) — the induced current direction is such that it opposes the change in magnetic flux that produced it. This is the minus sign in Faraday's Law (EMF = −dΦ/dt). Consistent with energy conservation — 'free' induced current would violate it. Practical example: dropping a magnet through a copper pipe — induced eddy currents oppose its fall, creating drag. Used in regenerative braking, induction cooktops, eddy-current brakes.

questions.stem: Materials that are STRONGLY attracted to magnets and can be permanently magnetised are called:
questions.explanation: Three basic magnetic categories — Ferromagnetic (Fe, Ni, Co, Gd, Dy, alloys like alnico, neodymium magnets) — strongly attracted, can retain magnetisation. Paramagnetic (Al, Pt, O₂) — weakly attracted, no retention. Diamagnetic (water, copper, gold, bismuth) — weakly REPELLED. Above the Curie temperature (Fe ~1043 K, Ni 627 K, Co 1394 K), ferromagnetic materials become paramagnetic. Antiferromagnetic — atomic magnetic moments align oppositely, cancel out (e.g., MnO).

questions.stem: An electromagnet differs from a permanent magnet because:

options.option_text: Its magnetism exists only when current flows through the coil; can be turned on/off
It is always weaker than a bar magnet
It does not need any iron core

questions.explanation: Electromagnet = solenoid (coil of insulated wire) wound around a soft-iron core. Magnetic field exists ONLY when current flows. Strength can be varied by current; can be very strong (MRI, particle accelerators, scrap-yard cranes). Soft iron is preferred (low retentivity → loses magnetism quickly when current stops; ideal for switchable devices). Permanent magnet uses high-coercivity materials (steel, neodymium-iron-boron) that retain magnetism without external current. Maglev trains use electromagnets for both lift and propulsion.
